modules.title: 1960 and 1963 Constitutions
modules.html:
1. Independence Constitution, 1960

  • Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a federation of three regions with Lagos as federal capital.
  • Parliamentary (Westminster) system: Queen Elizabeth II remained Head of State, represented by Governor-General Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe (from November 1960); Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was Prime Minister and head of government.
  • Bicameral federal legislature: Senate and House of Representatives.
  • Final appeal lay to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London.
  • Entrenched fundamental human rights (a response to the Willink Report).
  • Judicial Service Commission and constitutional safeguards for regions.

2. Republican Constitution, 1963

  • Nigeria became a Republic on 1 October 1963; the Queen ceased to be Head of State.
  • Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe became the first ceremonial President, elected by a joint session of parliament; Balewa remained Prime Minister.
  • Appeals to the Privy Council were abolished; the Supreme Court of Nigeria became the final court.
  • The Mid-Western Region was created in 1963, making four regions.
  • Retained the parliamentary system, federal structure and fundamental rights; the President was given emergency powers exercisable on the Prime Minister's advice.

3. Collapse of the First Republic

Census controversies (1962–63), the Western Region crisis and Operation Wetie, the treason trial of Awolowo, the disputed 1964 federal election and 1965 Western election, widespread violence and corruption culminated in the coup of 15 January 1966, the counter-coup of July 1966, and eventually the civil war of 1967–70.

examples.q: Distinguish the position of the Head of State in 1960 and in 1963.
examples.a: In 1960 the Head of State was the British monarch, Queen Elizabeth II, represented locally by a Governor-General; Nigeria was a constitutional monarchy within the Commonwealth. In 1963 Nigeria became a republic: the monarch was replaced by a Nigerian ceremonial President elected by parliament, sovereignty was fully localised, and appeals to the Privy Council ended. In both cases real executive power lay with the Prime Minister and cabinet.

examples.q: Why was the Mid-Western Region created in 1963?
examples.a: To answer minority agitation from the non-Yoruba peoples of the Western Region (Edo, Urhobo, Itsekiri, Ijaw, Isoko) whose fears the Willink Commission had documented, and — politically — to weaken the Action Group's Western power base at a time when the NPC/NCNC coalition controlled the centre. It became the only region created by the constitutional referendum procedure.

modules.title: 1979, 1989/1995 and 1999 Constitutions
modules.html:
1. The 1979 Constitution

  • Drafted by the Constitution Drafting Committee (1975–76) chaired by Chief Rotimi Williams and refined by a Constituent Assembly under Justice Udo Udoma; promulgated for the Second Republic on 1 October 1979.
  • Introduced the presidential system: an executive President who is both Head of State and Head of Government, directly elected with the two-thirds spread requirement.
  • Strict separation of powers with checks and balances; ministers not members of the legislature.
  • Bicameral National Assembly (Senate and House of Representatives) and 19 states.
  • Federal Character principle introduced to ensure inclusive appointments.
  • Chapter II Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles (non-justiciable); Chapter IV justiciable rights.
  • Parties required nationwide spread of membership and offices.

2. The 1989 and 1995 Documents

The 1989 Constitution was produced for Babangida's transition, retaining the presidential model and a decreed two-party system; it never fully operated because the 12 June 1993 election was annulled. The 1995 draft, from Abacha's Constitutional Conference, proposed rotational presidency among six zones and six vice-presidents; it was never promulgated.

3. The 1999 Constitution

  • Promulgated by Decree No. 24 of 1999 by General Abdulsalami Abubakar; in force from 29 May 1999.
  • Largely a restoration of the 1979 framework: presidential system, federalism with 36 states, the FCT and 774 local governments.
  • Section 1: supremacy of the constitution; section 14(2)(a): sovereignty belongs to the people.
  • Bicameral National Assembly: 109 senators (3 per state plus 1 for FCT) and 360 representatives.
  • Guaranteed democratically elected local government councils (section 7) and the State Joint Local Government Account (section 162(6)).
  • Independent institutions: INEC, Federal Character Commission, Code of Conduct Bureau and Tribunal, National Judicial Council.
  • Criticised for its military origin ('We the people' though not popularly ratified), over-centralisation of resources, and the exclusive list's length.

4. Comparative Summary

Feature1960/196319791999
SystemParliamentaryPresidentialPresidential
Head of StateQueen, then ceremonial PresidentExecutive PresidentExecutive President
Units3 then 4 regions19 states36 states + FCT
Final courtPrivy Council, then Supreme CourtSupreme CourtSupreme Court
OriginNegotiated with BritainCDC and Constituent AssemblyMilitary decree

examples.q: Why is the 1999 Constitution criticised as a 'military constitution'?
examples.a: It was promulgated by Decree No. 24 of 1999 under General Abdulsalami Abubakar without a referendum or an elected constituent assembly, and its preamble's claim that 'We the people... do hereby make, enact and give to ourselves' is therefore contested. Critics add that it entrenches a centralised federalism inherited from military command structures — a long Exclusive Legislative List, federal control of the police and mineral resources — which fuels demands for restructuring.

examples.q: State three innovations of the 1979 Constitution.
examples.a: (i) The executive presidency with direct election and the two-thirds spread requirement, replacing the Westminster model; (ii) the federal character principle, requiring that public appointments reflect national diversity; (iii) Chapter II Fundamental Objectives and Directive Principles, setting socio-economic goals of state policy, alongside a requirement that parties have national rather than regional character.

modules.title: The 1960 Independence Constitution
modules.html:
The 1960 Independence Constitution is a key part of Post-Independence Constitutions (1960–1999) (SSS 3, Government). Master the meaning, the main points and how it is tested in JAMB and WAEC questions on this topic.

Key points

  • Independence Constitution, 1960 Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a federation of three regions with Lagos as federal capital.
  • Parliamentary (Westminster) system : Queen Elizabeth II remained Head of State, represented by Governor-General Dr Nnamdi Azikiwe (from November 1960); Sir Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was Prime Minister and head of government.
  • Judicial Service Commission and constitutional safeguards for regions.
  • Republican Constitution, 1963 Nigeria became a Republic on 1 October 1963 ; the Queen ceased to be Head of State.
  • The 1979 Constitution Drafted by the Constitution Drafting Committee (1975–76) chaired by Chief Rotimi Williams and refined by a Constituent Assembly under Justice Udo Udoma; promulgated for the Second Republic on 1 October 1979 .

Worked example

Q: Nigeria became independent on:
A: 1 October 1960 — Independence was granted on 1 October 1960 within the Commonwealth.

Q: Under the 1960 Constitution the Head of State was:
A: The Queen represented by a Governor-General — Nigeria remained a constitutional monarchy until 1963.

examples.a: 1 October 1960 — Independence was granted on 1 October 1960 within the Commonwealth.

examples.q: Under the 1960 Constitution the Head of State was:
examples.a: The Queen represented by a Governor-General — Nigeria remained a constitutional monarchy until 1963.
